all_source_references.exact_span: B0 supplies \(\Re\rho\le7/8\) (OpenAIQRH, PDF p. 4, Theorem 1.1 and following paragraph). B1 implies \(\Re\rho\le27/32\) without needing any additional zero-free theorem. For \(\Re s>1\) the Euler product, logarithmic differentiation and integration by parts give

\[
 -\zeta'/\zeta(s)=s/(s-1)+s\int_1^\infty(\psi(t)-t)t^{-s-1}dt.
\]
The integral is analytic on \(\Re s>27/32\): its finite part has compact integration range, and on compact substrips the supplied \((1/64)t^{27/32}\log^2t\) majorant gives a uniform integrable bound even after differentiation. Meromorphic uniqueness excludes every zero there (a zero contributes a pole with nonzero residue). The boundary is not excluded. There is no nontrivial real zero: the alternating eta series is positive by pairing on \(0<s<1\), and equals \((1-2^{1-s})\zeta(s)\) by continuation (Dirichlet summation gives local uniform convergence on \(\Re s>0\)). This deduction affects estimates even for \(\log x<200\); the direct bound is not used at such \(x\).

B0 uses all seven pinned originals, at their stated analytic and computation trust. B1 adds exactly the all-real \(\psi\)-majorant in INPUT_CONTRACT.json. In particular, the additional input is not assumed below \(e^{200}\); its analytic continuation consequence \(\Re\rho\le27/32\) is used there where appropriate.

def coefficient(s,tighter=False):
 p=8*(1-s)/3
 q=5-2*s
 a=1-p
 # q<4; log(log H) enclosed via simple fixed rational endpoints
 lh=I(ln(Q(h.a,S)).a,ln(Q(h.b,S)).b,True)
 assert (h-I('28.72963')).yes() and (I('28.72964')-h).yes()
 z=1/(a-q/h)
 if tighter:
  assert 3<q<4
  f=Q(1);z=I(1)/a
  for j in range(1,5):
   f*=q-j+1
   z+=f/(a**(j+1)*h**j)
 return 2*(I('4.9')*exp(p*ln(3)+q*lh-a*h)*z+I('51.5')*(h*h+2*h+2)/H)
def spectral(beta,start=Q('.77'),step=Q('.001'),tighter=False):
 s=start; xs=[s]
 while s+step<beta:s+=step;xs.append(s)
 cs=[coefficient(x,tighter) for x in xs]+[I(0)]
 c=[(cs[j]-cs[j+1],0,1-y) for j,y in enumerate(xs[1:]+[beta])]
 assert all(t[0].yes() for t in c)
 return [(I(2),0,Q(1,2)),(I(13),1,Q(1,2)),(I(1)/24,2,Q(1,2)),(I(1),0,1-start),(I(1)/48,2,1-start)]+c
# Multiple alternative bin cutoffs retained when useful; margins certify the default .77 branch.
M0=spectral(B0);M1=spectral(B1)
CH=[(I('0.000000000001047198'),0,Q(0)),(I('113.67'),0,Q(1,2))]
POWER=[(I('1.000000147'),0,Q(1,2)),(I('1.78'),0,Q(2,3))]
FINE=[spectral(B0,step=Q('.000125')),spectral(B1,step=Q('.000125'))]

def coefficient(s,tighter=False):
 p=8*(1-s)/3
 q=5-2*s
 a=1-p
 # q<4; log(log H) enclosed via simple fixed rational endpoints
 lh=I(ln(Q(h.a,S)).a,ln(Q(h.b,S)).b,True)
 assert (h-I('28.72963')).yes() and (I('28.72964')-h).yes()
 z=1/(a-q/h)
 if tighter:
  assert 3<q<4
  f=Q(1);z=I(1)/a
  for j in range(1,5):
   f*=q-j+1
   z+=f/(a**(j+1)*h**j)
 return 2*(I('4.9')*exp(p*ln(3)+q*lh-a*h)*z+I('51.5')*(h*h+2*h+2)/H)
def spectral(beta,start=Q('.77'),step=Q('.001'),tighter=False):
 s=start; xs=[s]
 while s+step<beta:s+=step;xs.append(s)
 cs=[coefficient(x,tighter) for x in xs]+[I(0)]
 c=[(cs[j]-cs[j+1],0,1-y) for j,y in enumerate(xs[1:]+[beta])]
 assert all(t[0].yes() for t in c)
 return [(I(2),0,Q(1,2)),(I(13),1,Q(1,2)),(I(1)/24,2,Q(1,2)),(I(1),0,1-start),(I(1)/48,2,1-start)]+c

Thus \(\xi\) is exactly the unique root of \(632207037 e x/\log x=1644673232^2\) there. The gap is negative at the left endpoint, positive at the right, and strictly increasing on the unit interval. endpoint.py and primecount.cpp certify the counts, signs and bracket; the displayed expression also gives the exact local quantitative profile. The prime count code starts with \(g(w)=w-1\) on all distinct positive quotients \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\). Before the step at prime \(p\), it counts the primes below \(p\) together with integers \(\ge2\) with no prime factor below \(p\). It subtracts \(g(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-g(p-1)\) for \(w\ge p^2\), exactly the composites with least factor \(p\). The test \(g(p)>g(p-1)\) detects primes; quotient closure and descending \(w\) ensure use of unmodified subcounts. After processing through \(\sqrt n\), all composites are removed. This is independent of the published finite computation, but only for the three named integer arguments.

written_source.LF_text: At \(n_0\) and \(n_0+1\) the counts are both \(1644673232\), and throughout their intervening unit interval \(\lfloor x/e\rfloor=14111427770\) with count \(632207037\). Thus \(\xi\) is exactly the unique root of \(632207037 e x/\log x=1644673232^2\) there. The gap is negative at the left endpoint, positive at the right, and strictly increasing on the unit interval. endpoint.py and primecount.cpp certify the counts, signs and bracket; the displayed expression also gives the exact local quantitative profile. The prime count code starts with \(g(w)=w-1\) on all distinct positive quotients \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\). Before the step at prime \(p\), it counts the primes below \(p\) together with integers \(\ge2\) with no prime factor below \(p\). It subtracts \(g(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-g(p-1)\) for \(w\ge p^2\), exactly the composites with least factor \(p\). The test \(g(p)>g(p-1)\) detects primes; quotient closure and descending \(w\) ensure use of unmodified subcounts. After processing through \(\sqrt n\), all composites are removed. This is independent of the published finite computation, but only for the three named integer arguments.

all_source_references.exact_span: **Correction to the published real endpoint.** Let \(n_0=38358837682\). Platt–Trudgian 1809 PDF p. 3 Theorem 2 prints the range \(n_0<x\le e^{58}\). Read literally for every real number with inclusive \(\pi\), it is false, for example at \(x=38358837682.1\). We retain only its integer restriction and use monotonicity of \(R\) on every half-open interval \([n,n+1)\) with \(n>e\) (constant \(\pi(x)\), nondecreasing \(\pi(x/e)\), increasing \(x/\log x\)). This covers \([n_0+1,e^{58}]\) using the inherited finite statement for integers, and the new quantitative proof covers \([e^{36.73},\infty)\). This fills the gap to the published analytic onset \(e^{3915}\). Dudek–Platt 1407 PDF p. 2 Theorem 1.2 (\(x\ge e^{9658}\)) is subsumed. Their Theorem 1.3 assumes full RH and explicitly says *integer*. The real stepping argument in their Lemma 3.3 writes a bound by \(\varepsilon\) for the number of intervening primes; for general real endpoints the elementary available bound is \(\lceil\varepsilon\rceil\). We do not treat that as an independently corrected/reverified finite computation. If the inherited integer claim is removed, the short new endpoint computation and the analytic ray do not by themselves prove the intervening finite range.

The last eight rows take \(c=a_k\). There we subtract the first \(k+1\) terms, scale by \(L^{k+1}\) and check strict positivity rather than bounding \(a_k\) minus an error directly. The next coefficient is positive (including \(a_{15}=72793555607972000\)). In each tail certificate discard all subsequent positive terms, put subsequent negative terms at the onset, and bound the scaled error there: the log derivative of the power-exponential part is at most \((k'+4)/L+2/(L-1)-1/8<0\), where \(k'=k\) or \(k+1\). The factor \(L^{k'+4}h(L)\) decreases since \(k'+4<20\); the other factors used in the error are positive decreasing as in the earlier tail check. This proves the entire rays directly, without an untested finite interval. At the B0 onsets for the first six rows, B1 already admits the full \(a_k\) coefficient for \(k=7,\ldots,11\) by the later block (and the older results supply separate \(k=6\) tradeoffs). No constant \(c>a_k\) is possible in this exact fixed-order, fixed-prior-coefficients whole-ray shape: the same two-sided primitive bracket and exponential bound give \(L^k[L^6R/e^{2L}-\sum_{j<k}a_j/L^j]\to a_k\). def pconst(L,mode,fine=True):
 assert L>=40
 # Scaled envelope for A and H, including the entire raw prime-power tail.
 # Product error <= D exp(D) when |log normalized product| <= D.
 a=[Q(1,8),Q(5,32)][mode]
 m=(FINE if fine else [M0,M1])[mode]
 for c,d,b in m:assert d<=(b-a)*L
 # All scaled terms bounded by their values at L (decreasing polynomial*exponential).
 scale=ex(a*L)
 d=shifted(L,m,a)
 h=d+scale*(J(L,mode,0)+tail1(L))
 p=d+scale*(L*J(L,mode,1)+tail1(L))
 return h,p*(1+2*p*ex(-a*L)/L),p

def pc(L,b):
 assert L>=120
 a=[Q(1,8),Q(5,32)][b]
 assert Q(2)*L/(L*L-48*170)<Q('.23')-a
 assert all(d<=(r-a)*L for c,d,r in SP[b])
 g=spec(L,b,True)
 # For monotone tail use the original logarithmic theta tail majorant.
 j=Q('.1')*ex(-(Q(1,2)-a)*L)+Q('1e-11')+Q('2.1')*ex(-(1-a)*L)
 e2=Q('20.83')/(L/2)**3;e3=Q('20.83')/(L/3)**3
 tail=(1+3*e2)*ex(-(Q(1,2)-a)*L)+(2*(1+e3)+(1+5*e3)/2/(1-ex(-L/3)))*ex(-(Q(2,3)-a)*L)
 w=g+j+tail
 p=g+(1+1/L)*j+tail
 assert p.yes() and (1-p).yes()
 return w,p*(1+2*p*ex(-a*L)/L),p

def pconst(L,mode,fine=True):
 assert L>=40
 # Scaled envelope for A and H, including the entire raw prime-power tail.
 # Product error <= D exp(D) when |log normalized product| <= D.
 a=[Q(1,8),Q(5,32)][mode]
 m=(FINE if fine else [M0,M1])[mode]
 for c,d,b in m:assert d<=(b-a)*L
 # All scaled terms bounded by their values at L (decreasing polynomial*exponential).
 scale=ex(a*L)
 d=shifted(L,m,a)
 h=d+scale*(J(L,mode,0)+tail1(L))
 p=d+scale*(L*J(L,mode,1)+tail1(L))
 return h,p*(1+2*p*ex(-a*L)/L),p

For every row \((\mathrm{mode},u,c)\) in mertens.py, with \(a=1/8\) in B0 and \(a=5/32\) in B1, the following hold for all \(x\ge e^u\):
\[
 |E_W|\le c x^{-a},\qquad
 |E_S|,\ |e^\gamma L P_{\rm raw}-1|,\ |e^{-\gamma}Q_{\rm raw}/L-1|
       \le c x^{-a}/L .
\]
There are also the early-envelope rows \((0,40,.01334)\) and \((1,40,.2665)\). The certificate evaluates \(e^{a u}G_b(u)\); \(e^{aL}G_b(L)\) thereafter decreases termwise (weakly for the top rate), and so do the appropriately scaled tail/oscillatory corrections \(e^{aL}(J_H+U_1)\), \(e^{aL}(LJ_A+U_1)\). If the log-product radius is \(D\le1/2\), both relative errors are \(\le D(1+2D)\). For the early-envelope rows, on the interval up to the listed pivot \(v\) bound the renormalized CH2 constant term by its value at \(v\) and the renormalized square-root term by its value at 40. Use the spectral proof starting at the pivot. This ensures both joins and the full infinite ray. The code represents the real exponent \(a\) exactly. For example, at \(\log x=200\), the B1 coefficient .222 suffices; at 300 it is .172. This replaces the logarithmic loss of the direct assumption rather than just tightening its coefficient. Constants with later domains are kept when stronger pointwise.

For two such branches with coefficients \(c_0,c_1\), the B1 branch improves the B0 branch exactly when \(L>32\log(c_1/c_0)\), on the intersection of the stated domains (equality is a tie). For the primary smoothed pointwise branch using \(\min(C,G_b)\), the B1 envelope is never worse; from \(L=170\) its \(\delta\) radius is strictly smaller (verify against the CH2 floor at 170 and use monotonicity; clipping shows strict improvement against \(G_{7/8}\)). Its \(J\) terms are also smaller. Hence the primary absolute envelopes improve strictly on this ray for both product errors and both sums. Earlier or competing finite-source/transfer branches are handled by intersection, not assumed strictly improved. At large \(L\) the matched original logarithmic and stretched-exponential error branches are weaker than the B0 exponential reconstruction, not a suitable substitute for it. The reconstructed bounds are not claimed optimal over all proofs possible from B0.

def pconst(L,mode,fine=True):
 assert L>=40
 # Scaled envelope for A and H, including the entire raw prime-power tail.
 # Product error <= D exp(D) when |log normalized product| <= D.
 a=[Q(1,8),Q(5,32)][mode]
 m=(FINE if fine else [M0,M1])[mode]
 for c,d,b in m:assert d<=(b-a)*L
 # All scaled terms bounded by their values at L (decreasing polynomial*exponential).
 scale=ex(a*L)
 d=shifted(L,m,a)
 h=d+scale*(J(L,mode,0)+tail1(L))
 p=d+scale*(L*J(L,mode,1)+tail1(L))
 return h,p*(1+2*p*ex(-a*L)/L),p

For every row \((\mathrm{mode},u,c)\) in mertens.py, with \(a=1/8\) in B0 and \(a=5/32\) in B1, the following hold for all \(x\ge e^u\):
\[
 |E_W|\le c x^{-a},\qquad
 |E_S|,\ |e^\gamma L P_{\rm raw}-1|,\ |e^{-\gamma}Q_{\rm raw}/L-1|
       \le c x^{-a}/L .
\]
There are also the early-envelope rows \((0,40,.01334)\) and \((1,40,.2665)\). The certificate evaluates \(e^{a u}G_b(u)\); \(e^{aL}G_b(L)\) thereafter decreases termwise (weakly for the top rate), and so do the appropriately scaled tail/oscillatory corrections \(e^{aL}(J_H+U_1)\), \(e^{aL}(LJ_A+U_1)\). If the log-product radius is \(D\le1/2\), both relative errors are \(\le D(1+2D)\). For the early-envelope rows, on the interval up to the listed pivot \(v\) bound the renormalized CH2 constant term by its value at \(v\) and the renormalized square-root term by its value at 40. Use the spectral proof starting at the pivot. This ensures both joins and the full infinite ray. The code represents the real exponent \(a\) exactly. For example, at \(\log x=200\), the B1 coefficient .222 suffices; at 300 it is .172. This replaces the logarithmic loss of the direct assumption rather than just tightening its coefficient. Constants with later domains are kept when stronger pointwise.

For two such branches with coefficients \(c_0,c_1\), the B1 branch improves the B0 branch exactly when \(L>32\log(c_1/c_0)\), on the intersection of the stated domains (equality is a tie). This applies to each of the four quantities with its matching logarithmic factor. For the primary smoothed pointwise branch using \(\min(C,G_b)\), the B1 envelope is never worse; from \(L=170\) its \(\delta\) radius is strictly smaller (verify against the CH2 floor at 170 and use monotonicity; clipping shows strict improvement against \(G_{7/8}\)). Its \(J\) terms are also smaller. Hence the primary absolute envelopes improve strictly on this ray for both product errors and both sums. Earlier or competing finite-source/transfer branches are handled by intersection, not assumed strictly improved. At large \(L\) the matched original logarithmic and stretched-exponential error branches are weaker than the B0 exponential reconstruction, not a suitable substitute for it. The reconstructed bounds are not claimed optimal over all proofs possible from B0.

**Mertens.** Preserve all supported signed intervals, finite real improvements on original Dusart endpoints, and all power/log menus in mertens.md. The new density and oscillatory estimates in enhanced.md improve the whole-domain pointwise minima, and give, under B1, constants \(.21726x^{-5/32}\) for the centered weighted sum and \(.21726x^{-5/32}/L\) for both relative product errors and the centered reciprocal sum on \(L\ge200\). The former .222 now applies from 196; the former .172 from 288. The corresponding B0 exponent is \(1/8\) with its own constants. New early rays begin at \(x=368359\) in B0 and \(L=10\) in B1. Exact ratios and signed intersections preserve stronger branches on matched domains. Both product errors and sums are correlated, not independent trials.

No implication across unequal exponents is inferred from constants alone.

all_source_references.exact_span: For differing pure logarithmic exponents the comparison is exactly the comparison of \(L^{k_1-k_0}\) with the ratio of the constants, reversing when testing the opposite inequality. To compare a power-exponential bound \(c x^{-a}/L^d\) with \(\eta/L^k\), compare the ratio \((c/\eta)L^{k-d}e^{-aL}\) with 1. It is decreasing for \(L>(k-d)/a\), so after this point one verified endpoint comparison gives whole-ray dominance, and otherwise any crossing there is unique. Before that point it is increasing when \(k>d\), so the turning point and the matching domain suffice. In particular the B0 exponential bounds already improve Dusart's .2 and .3 bounds for every \(L\ge40\) (insert the early B0 row at 40, then use the decreasing ratio). B1 does not replace the earlier finite-source branches.

For two such branches with coefficients \(c_0,c_1\), the B1 branch improves the B0 branch exactly when \(L>32\log(c_1/c_0)\), on the intersection of the stated domains (equality is a tie). This applies to each of the four quantities with its matching logarithmic factor. For the primary smoothed pointwise branch using \(\min(C,G_b)\), the B1 envelope is never worse; from \(L=170\) its \(\delta\) radius is strictly smaller (verify against the CH2 floor at 170 and use monotonicity; clipping shows strict improvement against \(G_{7/8}\)). Its \(J\) terms are also smaller. Hence the primary absolute envelopes improve strictly on this ray for both product errors and both sums. Earlier or competing finite-source/transfer branches are handled by intersection, not assumed strictly improved. At large \(L\) the matched original logarithmic and stretched-exponential error branches are weaker than the B0 exponential reconstruction, not a suitable substitute for it. The reconstructed bounds are not claimed optimal over all proofs possible from B0.

all_source_references.exact_span: Keep everything in the original signed comparison and take the minima with this supplement. The matched simple powers have their exact cross-mode comparison \(e^{L/32}>c_1/c_0\), when both apply. For the **two exhibited early rows** this gives the unique crossing \(32\log(.2612/.01318)\) on the common domain; the earlier B1 branch has no strict advantage over the stronger B0 minima there merely by having a larger exponent. From \(L\ge140\), the B1 .34621 row beats every B0 row of the two displayed simple exponential menus (even against the smallest B0 coefficient .006750 extrapolated back only for the comparison, not as a bound); the strict 140 test is in enhanced.py, and the ratio decreases. For log-power and original-source comparisons use the ratios and domains in mertens.md; this never drops a stronger original input. In particular the pure-log/pointwise branches can win earlier than the simple power rows. This is a within-method ablation, not an independently blind baseline and not a claim to exhaust possible deductions from the original packet. The common-source cutoffs, power-tail limits, finite joins and direct error conversions do not need D02; the B1 improvements in the spectral and oscillatory branches use exactly the narrower strip obtained from it.

all_source_references.exact_span: Either relative product bound of the same rate gives the latter \(E_S\) estimate by taking a logarithm for large \(x\) and using \(E_S=Z+U_0\). Prime-power correction makes \(\psi(x)-x=O(x^{1-\alpha})\), and the integral continuation argument in common.md then excludes zeros with \(\Re\rho>1-\alpha\). Thus improving the power (with the stated log factors) for any of these four quantities would itself imply a stronger zero-free half-plane. This does not rule out proving one under the given premises; it explains why tighter real joins, density constants, and better oscillatory tail integration alone do not supply a proved larger exponent.
